title: OGL v3 Attribution Specification — HM Land Registry Price Paid Data & UK House Price Index (public web game)
rules: Display HM Land Registry's OWN specified attribution statement, not the generic OGL one — OGL v3 requires you to 'acknowledge the source of the Information in your product or application by including or linking to any attribution statement specified by the Information Provider(s)', and HMLR has specified one.
Use the HMLR-mandated sentence verbatim for both datasets: 'Contains HM Land Registry data © Crown copyright and database right [year]. This data is licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0.'

Set [year] to the year of supply or date of publication of the data you actually shipped — data.gov.uk states the placeholder literally as '[year of supply or date of publication]'. For data fetched live in 2026, that is 2026.

Hyperlink the phrase 'Open Government Licence v3.0' to https://www.nationalarchives.gov.uk/doc/open-government-licence/version/3/ — linking the licence is the cleanest way to satisfy the acknowledgement requirement.

Where a small footer cannot carry both full statements, OGL v3 expressly permits: 'If you are using Information from several Information Providers and listing multiple attributions is not practical in your product or application, you may include a URI or hyperlink to a resource that contains the required attribution statements.' Link a dedicated /attribution page.
Keep the attribution visible in the product itself (footer, about screen, or a linked attribution page reachable from every page) — not buried in a repo README or source comment.

Credit UKHPI's joint production correctly: it is produced by HM Land Registry, Registers of Scotland, Land and Property Services Northern Ireland and the Office for National Statistics, using ONS's hedonic regression model.

Respect the Royal Mail / Ordnance Survey carve-out on PPD address fields: permitted use is 'for personal and/or non-commercial use' or 'to display for the purpose of providing residential property price information services'; anything else requires written permission from Royal Mail (address.management@royalmail.com).
Treat these PPD fields as the restricted Address Data: Postcode, PAON, SAON, Street, Locality, Town/City, District, County.

Carry the 'as is' position through to your own terms — OGL v3 states the Information is licensed 'as is' and the Information Provider excludes all representations, warranties, obligations and liabilities to the maximum extent permitted by law.
State a data-currency line (dataset name and extract date) alongside the attribution, since UKHPI figures are revised as later transactions register.
Comply with the Data Protection Act 2018 and PECR in your use of the data — HMLR states users have this obligation under the OGL.
Reproduce the '©' character and the full stops exactly; do not restyle to '(c)', 'Copyright', or drop the trailing full stop.
Re-check the attribution wording on gov.uk at each major release — HMLR has changed the example year across pages, and the licence terms are the publisher's to revise.
antiPatterns: Shipping ONLY 'Contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0.' — that is the OGL default for when a provider specifies nothing; HMLR specifies its own statement, so the generic line alone under-attributes.
Displaying full street addresses (PAON/SAON/Street/Postcode) in a monetised or advertising-supported public game — that is outside the two permitted Address Data uses and needs Royal Mail permission.

Building an address-lookup, address-autocomplete, address-validation or address-cleansing feature out of PPD address fields — squarely outside the permitted uses and a Royal Mail PAF licensing breach.
Redistributing the PPD address fields as a bulk downloadable dataset, public API, or scrapeable JSON endpoint from your game.
Omitting the year, or hard-coding a stale year copied from a gov.uk example (2020 and 2021 both appear on live HMLR pages) instead of the year of supply or publication of your extract.
Writing '© Crown Copyright' with a capital C on 'copyright', or dropping 'and database right' — the database right is a separate, expressly claimed right.
Claiming your own copyright over the underlying data (e.g. '© YourGame 2026' next to the figures, with no HMLR line) — you may own your presentation, not the data.
Implying HM Land Registry, ONS, Registers of Scotland or LPS NI endorses, sponsors or verifies the game — OGL v3 prohibits using the Information in a way that suggests official status or endorsement.
Reproducing the Royal Arms, HM Land Registry or ONS logos or crests — expressly exempted from the OGL and not licensed to you.

Joining PPD to electoral roll, Companies House PSC, social media or other datasets to name the buyer or seller of a specific property, then publishing that — OGL exempts personal data, and this creates re-identification and DPA 2018 exposure.
Using the data to build direct-marketing lists targeting occupiers of identified properties — HMLR reserves the right to restrict this and PECR/DPA still bite.
Putting attribution only in an HTML comment, a meta tag, alt text, or a hidden/collapsed element — it must be a visible acknowledgement.
Presenting UKHPI as 'HM Land Registry house prices' with no mention of ONS, Registers of Scotland or LPS NI — misattributes a jointly produced statistic.
Presenting UKHPI figures as final and unrevisable, or PPD as a complete record of all sales — sales excluded from registration are omitted from PPD.
Copying the OGL text into your own terms and calling it your licence, or sublicensing the data onward under different terms.

notes:
PERSONAL DATA AND RE-IDENTIFICATION

1. OGL v3 does not licence personal data at all. Its Exemptions list opens with "personal data in the Information". So nothing in the OGL cures a data protection problem you create by combining PPD with other sources.

2. HMLR's stated position, verbatim: "Price Paid Data is not personal information about individuals but property related information." That is HMLR's characterisation of the raw dataset — it is not a blanket indemnity for what you build on top of it. PPD rows pair a full address with a price and a date; combined with any source naming an occupier (electoral roll, Companies House PSC, LinkedIn, social media, the game's own user accounts), that becomes personal data about an identifiable living individual, and you become the controller of it.

3. HMLR's own stated obligation on reusers, verbatim: "The users of the data have an obligation, under the Open Government Licence, to ensure that their use of the data does not breach the Data Protection Act 2018 or the Privacy and Electronic Communication (EC Directive) Regulations 2003."

4. Direct marketing, verbatim: "At the moment, we do not intend to impose any more restrictions on the use of the data for direct marketing purpose." Read that as a reserved right, not permission — the phrase is "at the moment". DPA 2018 and PECR still apply regardless.

5. Practical design guidance for a public guessing game: never let a player look up a named person; never surface a specific transaction keyed to a real household in a way that invites "who lives there" speculation; do not offer address search or reverse lookup; do not let users comment on or tag specific addresses. Prefer coarse geography (town, district, outward postcode sector) and aggregated or sampled data over full addresses. This also keeps you inside the Royal Mail address-data carve-out.

THE BIGGEST PRACTICAL RISK IS NOT THE OGL — IT IS THE ROYAL MAIL / ORDNANCE SURVEY ADDRESS CARVE-OUT

PPD is OGL-licensed, but the address fields inside it are not fully yours. Verbatim from the HMLR Price Paid Data downloads page:

"Royal Mail and Ordnance Survey permit your use of Address Data in the Price Paid Data:
- for personal and/or non-commercial use
- to display for the purpose of providing residential property price information services
If you want to use the Address Data in any other way, you must contact Royal Mail. Email address.management@royalmail.com."

And the fields caught, verbatim: "Postcode, PAON Primary Addressable Object Name (typically the house number or name), SAON Secondary Addressable Object Name..., Street, Locality, Town/City, District, County."

A public web game that displays real addresses sits in a genuinely grey zone. If it is free and unmonetised it plausibly reads as non-commercial. The moment it carries advertising, sponsorship, a paid tier, or is a lead-generation asset for the consultancy, the non-commercial limb falls away and you are relying entirely on the second limb — "providing residential property price information services" — which is a stretch for a game. Two clean routes out: (a) drop the granular address fields and play on town/district/outward-postcode plus price, which removes the exposure entirely; or (b) email address.management@royalmail.com and get written permission before launch. I would take route (a).

YEAR IN THE ATTRIBUTION

The canonical form on data.gov.uk is "[year of supply or date of publication]". Live gov.uk pages contradict each other on the worked example — the Price Paid Data downloads page shows 2021, the About the UK House Price Index page shows 2020. Both are stale examples, not the required value. Use the year you took your extract: 2026. Wire the year off a build-time constant so it cannot silently rot.

ONE MORE THING WORTH CHECKING BEFORE LAUNCH

The two UKHPI URLs behave differently: https://landregistry.data.gov.uk/app/ukhpi 301-redirects to the http:// form with a trailing slash. Pin your fetches to the trailing-slash form and force HTTPS at your end, so a redirect chain never silently drops you onto plain HTTP in production.
